message: Your brief is in BRIEF.md in this folder. Your last message is your reply: the painting's title if you give it one and a few sentences about the picture. At the end of each sitting, leave a handoff in your journal and last reply: passages still unresolved, practical lessons to carry forward from what you observed and recipes that failed. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Carry forward the conditions of material trials and repairs: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, load, coverage and viewed result; label broader rules as hypotheses. final:
I've finished the painting and called it **The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines**. It's on a 73 cm linen canvas, painted over about five and a half months of simulated time, and I signed it in the lower left.

**The picture.** Two umbrella pines stand on the left. Their crowns run across the top of the canvas and their trunks frame a broad plain. On the plain is a hill village: cubic ochre-and-cream houses with red-tile roofs, grouped among dark trees. Behind it rises a pale mountain, lit rose and ochre on its left slope and violet on the shaded face. A road comes up from the bottom edge and runs into the village. The pines' blue-violet shadows lie across the road and the green and gold meadow, and a dark bush closes the lower right corner.

**How it was built.** I started with a dilute ultramarine drawing and thin washes. After that, almost everything was built from patches of short, parallel flat-brush strokes laid over dry paint. Each patch has its own colour and direction, and I kept the colours warm against cool rather than modelling with light and dark. The sky, plain and mountain ended up as a mosaic of these patches. Broken blue lines mark the mountain ridge, and muted violet lines mark the shadow sides of the trunks.

**Still unresolved:**
- The mountain is too symmetrical, close to a plain cone.
- The houses still look a little cut-out at their edges.
- One trunk has a stray thin blue line beside it, and both trunks are straighter and more parallel than I'd like.
- The middle of the right-hand meadow is a flat yellow-green.

**Lessons carried forward (most are hypotheses):**
- **Best patch method:** the strongest Cézanne-like structure came from patch passes laid over dry paint, with no gap-filling dabs. I used a flat brush 7–12 units wide, strokes 14–46 long, about one layer of coverage, and the colour chosen patch by patch.
- **Failed recipe:** filling in the gaps between strokes while mixing several piles over half-dry paint (still tacky or setting) turned the foreground into a soft smear. That was seen once, on day 12.
- **Rag and knife:**
  - A rag dipped in solvent lifted thin, freshly laid lines cleanly, using several wipes and refolds.
  - Neither the rag nor a hard knife scrape lifted much from thick fresh hatching.
- **Chalky lights:** foreground mixes with more than about two parts lead white looked chalky over the greens. Warm, pigment-rich lights worked better there.
- **Wall shadows:** shadow planes on the pale walls needed three overlays before they read as shadow.

The full conditions for each trial and repair, and the handoff, are in `notes/journal.md`.

final:
The painting is finished: **The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines**.

Two umbrella pines on the left frame a plain of patchwork fields. Cubic ochre-and-cream houses with red-tile roofs stand among dark trees. A road leads up to them through blue-violet pine shadows, and a pale rose-and-violet mountain rises behind. Everything is built from short, parallel flat-brush strokes in warm and cool patches.

**What I changed this sitting:**
- **Mountain:** my main worry was that it looked like a plain cone. It now has a long right shoulder, with a small knoll, a cool violet plane under the dip and broken blue ridge lines. This made it lopsided and gave the right half of the picture the weight it lacked.
- **Houses:** I added cast shadows and dark strips at their bases so they sit on the ground. I also gave the shadow walls a stone texture and softened the dark tree edges around them.
- **Trunk and canopy lines:** I painted over the stray blue line beside the left trunk, so that stretch of trunk is now continuous and round. I also covered thin blue lines across the canopy that read as wires.
- **Right meadow:** the flat yellow-green stretch is now a mosaic of greens, ochres and cool patches.

**Accepted as they are:** the trunks are still fairly straight and parallel, the house edges are crisp, and the canopy's pattern repeats a little. I left these on purpose. They suit the picture's plain, built-up character, and reworking them risked more than it would gain.

**New lesson:** a rag lifts a fresh line cleanly, but it also lifts any wet paint underneath. When I wiped a line off the mountain, it took up the violet laid minutes before. So I'll only put lines on dry paint if I might want to wipe them.

All the paint was dry at day 185. My journal has a judgement on each passage I'd left unresolved and an updated handoff. My heart is happy with this one.

final:
**The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines** is finished.

I came back to it with fresh eyes and the picture still holds. The two umbrella pines frame a plain of patchwork fields, and cream-and-ochre houses with red roofs sit among dark trees. Behind them a rose-and-violet mountain with a long right shoulder carries the right half of the picture. Everything is built from short, parallel strokes in warm and cool patches.

**What I changed:** the one passage I'd noted as unresolved but never judged was the sunlit upper stretch of the road. It was a pale wedge with a ruler-straight right edge. Earlier I had tried feathering that edge, but that kept the straight line and only added a strip of acid lime. This time I redrew the edge instead:
- Small patches of meadow green cut into the road along the edge.
- In other places, small patches of road colour push out into the grass.

Now the road's top runs naturally into the grass. A few of the pale dabs outside the edge are slightly too many, but they read as stones or dust and don't show at full view, so I left them.

**Accepted as they are:**
- The thin blue lines along the house edges. I checked them up close: they read as Cézanne-style blue drawing and are barely visible at full view.
- The fairly straight trunks, the crisp house edges and the repeating canopy pattern, for the same reasons as last time.

Everything was dry by day 197. My journal has a judgement on each passage and an updated handoff with the lessons that still apply. My heart is happy with the painting. If I came back, the one thing I'd enjoy taking further is giving the trunks more movement. I'd only do that as a planned rework of both trunks, not as patching.

final:
**The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines** is finished.

Last time I said the one thing I'd enjoy taking further was the stiffness of the two pine trunks. This sitting I rebuilt both of them as one planned campaign, not as patching.

**What I changed:**
- **New trunk lines:** I drew a new curving centreline for each trunk. The near pine now leans out at its base, straightens through the middle and turns into its canopy. The far pine leans gently the other way. The two curves are different, so the trunks no longer look like a matched pair.
- **Covering the old trunks:** first I tested on the scratch canvas how to hide the old orange trunks. A dense filling pass covered them completely in one go, but on the painting it left smooth vertical blocks. Once that was dry, I broke the blocks up with the same mosaic of short patch strokes I used elsewhere in the plain and sky, in wider bands that cross the blocks' edges. Seen with blurred eyes, the ghosts are gone.
- **Bark:** I tested three bark mixtures on the scratch canvas first and picked the gentlest. The bark is painted in four bands of warm-to-cool colour across each trunk, with broken strokes on top in pink, earth and green. A later pass calmed some violet spots that looked blotchy.
- **Limbs:** short limbs now fork from the trunk tops into the foliage, partly covered by leaves so only pieces of branch show.

**Accepted as they are:** the crisp house edges and the repeating rhythm of the canopy. Both belong to the picture's plain, built quality.

**Still uncertain:** a faint trace of the old straight trunks might remain under the plain up close, but I can't see it at full view or with blurred eyes.

Everything was dry by day 254. My journal has a judgement on each passage and an updated handoff with the lessons that still apply. My heart is happy with it: the pines move a little now, and the left half has some of the life the mountain gives the right.

final:
**The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines** is finished. All the paint was dry by day 263.

When I came back I looked at the whole canvas and close-ups, and the picture still holds. I checked again for traces of the old straight trunks under the plain and couldn't see any, even at full detail.

**What I changed:** I found one weak spot I hadn't noticed before. The top of the smaller pine was under a pale sky-coloured film left by an old sky pass, so it looked like mist instead of foliage. Over the dry paint I laid broken patches of warm light greens and mid greens, kept inside the canopy so its outline didn't change. Now that crown catches the light from the upper left as the bigger pine does, so the two trees agree about where the sun is.

**Accepted as they are:**
- **A thin dark streak** under the small pine's canopy reads as a twig.
- **A pale gap of sky** in that canopy stays.
- **A small violet patch** at the left edge picks up the violet of the road shadows.
- **The crisp house edges and the repeating rhythm of the canopy** belong to the picture's plain, built quality.

My heart is happy with it. The only thing I might look at again is whether the upper-right sky is too busy, but today I think it belongs to the picture. The journal has the judgements and an updated handoff with the lessons that still apply.

final:
**The Village below the Mountain, with Two Pines** is finished as it stood. I didn't lay any paint this sitting.

I looked at the whole canvas and at full-detail close-ups of the upper-right sky, the smaller pine's crown, both halves of the foreground, the shadowed road and the village.

- **Upper-right sky:** last time I left open whether it was too busy. I've decided to keep it as it is. Its broken, tilted patches give the right side some movement against the heavy pine canopy at upper left and the mountain's calm planes. If I quietened it, that half of the picture would go flat.
- **Small pine's crown:** last sitting's repair still works. Its lit top agrees with the big pine about where the sun is.
- **Shadowed road:** green and ochre patches already break up its edges, so there's no ruled line to fix.
- **Houses:** I still accept their crisp edges as part of the picture's plain, built quality.

My heart is happy with it, and I can't see anything I'd enjoy taking further. More marks now would just be fiddling. The journal has this sitting's judgements and the handoff, with the practical lessons that still apply:
- broken patch strokes laid over dry paint
- breaking up straight edges by working across them
- what a rag can and can't lift
- keeping foreground lights warm rather than chalky
- three shadow layers on pale walls
- always masking out neighbouring objects
